blocks.text: 29.18 External Audio Effect
blocks.raw_html: 29.18 External Audio Effect

blocks.text: The External Audio Effect is a bit different than Live’s other effects devices. Instead of processing audio itself, it allows you to use external (hardware) effects processors within a track’s device chain.
blocks.raw_html: The External Audio Effect is a bit different than Live’s other effects devices. Instead of processing audio itself, it allows you to use external (hardware) effects processors within a track’s device chain.

blocks.text: The Audio To chooser selects the outputs on your computer’s audio hardware that will go to your external device, while the Audio From chooser selects the inputs that will bring the processed signal back into Live. As with the track inputs and outputs, the list of available inputs and outputs depends on the Audio Settings, which can be reached via the ”Configure…” option at the bottom of each chooser.
blocks.raw_html: The Audio To chooser selects the outputs on your computer’s audio hardware that will go to your external device, while the Audio From chooser selects the inputs that will bring the processed signal back into Live. As with the track inputs and outputs, the list of available inputs and outputs depends on the Audio Settings, which can be reached via the ”Configure…” option at the bottom of each chooser.

blocks.text: Below each chooser is a Peak level indicator that shows the highest audio level attained. Click on the indicators to reset them.
blocks.raw_html: Below each chooser is a Peak level indicator that shows the highest audio level attained. Click on the indicators to reset them.

blocks.text: The Gain knobs next to the choosers adjust the levels going out of and back into Live. These levels should be set carefully to avoid clipping, both in your external hardware and when returning the audio to your computer.
blocks.raw_html: The Gain knobs next to the choosers adjust the levels going out of and back into Live. These levels should be set carefully to avoid clipping, both in your external hardware and when returning the audio to your computer.

blocks.text: The Dry/Wet control adjusts the balance between the processed and dry signals. Set it to 100 percent if using the External Audio Effect in a return track.
blocks.raw_html: The Dry/Wet control adjusts the balance between the processed and dry signals. Set it to 100 percent if using the External Audio Effect in a return track.

blocks.text: The Invert button inverts the phase of the processed signal coming back into Live.
blocks.raw_html: The Invert button inverts the phase of the processed signal coming back into Live.

blocks.text: Since hardware effects introduce latency that Live cannot automatically detect, you can manually compensate for any delays by adjusting the Hardware Latency slider. The button next to this slider allows you to set your latency compensation amount in either milliseconds or samples. If your external device connects to Live via a digital connection, you will want to adjust your latency settings in samples, which ensures that the number of samples you specify will be retained even when changing the sample rate. If your external device connects to Live via an analog connection, you will want to adjust your latency settings in milliseconds, which ensures that the amount of time you specify will be retained when changing the sample rate. Note that adjusting in samples gives you finer control, so even in cases when you’re working with analog devices, you may want to ”fine tune” your latency in samples in order to achieve the lowest possible latency. In this case, be sure to switch back to milliseconds before changing your sample rate.

blocks.text: 31.6 External Instrument
blocks.raw_html: 31.6 External Instrument

blocks.text: The External Instrument device is not an instrument itself, but rather a routing utility that allows you to easily integrate external (hardware) synthesizers and multitimbral plug-ins into your projects. It sends MIDI out and returns audio.
blocks.raw_html: The External Instrument device is not an instrument itself, but rather a routing utility that allows you to easily integrate external (hardware) synthesizers and multitimbral plug-ins into your projects. It sends MIDI out and returns audio.

blocks.text: The two MIDI To choosers select the output to which the device will send MIDI data. The top chooser selects either a physical MIDI port, or a multitimbral plug-in. If you select a MIDI port (for use with an external synthesizer), the second chooser’s options will be MIDI channel numbers.
blocks.raw_html: The two MIDI To choosers select the output to which the device will send MIDI data. The top chooser selects either a physical MIDI port, or a multitimbral plug-in. If you select a MIDI port (for use with an external synthesizer), the second chooser’s options will be MIDI channel numbers.

blocks.text: If another track in your Set contains a multitimbral plug-in, you can select this track in the top chooser. In this case, the second chooser allows you to select a specific MIDI channel in the plug-in.
blocks.raw_html: If another track in your Set contains a multitimbral plug-in, you can select this track in the top chooser. In this case, the second chooser allows you to select a specific MIDI channel in the plug-in.

blocks.text: The Audio From chooser provides options for returning the audio from the hardware synth or plug-in device. If you’re routing to a hardware synth, use this chooser to select the ports on your audio interface that are connected to the output of your synth. The available choices you’ll have will depend on the settings in the Audio Settings.
blocks.raw_html: The Audio From chooser provides options for returning the audio from the hardware synth or plug-in device. If you’re routing to a hardware synth, use this chooser to select the ports on your audio interface that are connected to the output of your synth. The available choices you’ll have will depend on the settings in the Audio Settings.

blocks.text: If you’re routing to a multitimbral plug-in on another track in your Live Set, the Audio From chooser will list the auxiliary outputs in the plug-in. Note that the main outputs will be heard on the track that contains the instrument.
blocks.raw_html: If you’re routing to a multitimbral plug-in on another track in your Live Set, the Audio From chooser will list the auxiliary outputs in the plug-in. Note that the main outputs will be heard on the track that contains the instrument.

blocks.text: The Gain knob adjusts the audio level coming back from the sound source. This level should be set carefully to avoid clipping.
blocks.raw_html: The Gain knob adjusts the audio level coming back from the sound source. This level should be set carefully to avoid clipping.

blocks.text: Since external devices can introduce latency that Live cannot automatically detect, you can manually compensate for any delays by adjusting the Hardware Latency slider. The button next to this slider allows you to set your latency compensation amount in either milliseconds or samples. If your external device connects to Live via a digital connection, you will want to adjust your latency settings in samples, which ensures that the number of samples you specify will be retained even when changing the sample rate. If your external device connects to Live via an analog connection, you will want to adjust your latency settings in milliseconds, which ensures that the amount of time you specify will be retained when changing the sample rate. Note that adjusting in samples gives you finer control, so even in cases when you’re working with analog devices, you may want to “fine tune“ your latency in samples in order to achieve the lowest possible latency. In this case, be sure to switch back to milliseconds before changing your sample rate. Any latency introduced by devices within Live will be compensated for automatically, so the slider will be disabled when using the External Instrument Device to route internally.

owner_requirements.contract: With External Audio Effect in an audio path, Audio To selects physical audio outputs to the external processor and Audio From selects physical inputs returning its processed signal. This is a hardware-routing effect; the section supplies no internal effect algorithm.

Available Audio To and Audio From choices depend on Audio Settings. Configure… at the bottom of each chooser reaches those settings. No complete port domain, mono/stereo grouping, order or unavailable-port policy is specified.

A Peak level indicator below each chooser shows the highest attained audio level; clicking an indicator resets it. Measurement convention, observation window, reset sentinel and update timing are unknown.
Separate Gain knobs beside the choosers adjust the level going out to the processor and the level coming back into Live. Gain domains, dB-to-amplitude law and clipping behavior are unknown.

Dry/Wet controls the balance of dry and externally processed signals; the manual recommends 100% when placed on a return track. This recommendation is not a mandatory insertion setting or a specified mixing law.
Invert applies phase inversion to the processed signal returning into Live. No phase convention, channel matrix, numeric negation rule or dry-path sample comparator is established.

Hardware Latency allows manual compensation for hardware delay not automatically detected by Live. Its adjacent button selects milliseconds or samples. Sample fine tuning followed by a return to milliseconds before a rate change is documented guidance; conversion, range and precision are unknown.
When Hardware Latency is set in samples, the specified sample count is retained across a sample-rate change. The selected count is the state observation, not a promised measured hardware delay.
When Hardware Latency is set in milliseconds, the specified duration is retained across a sample-rate change. No sample conversion, rounding or compensation implementation is specified.
Unchecking Delay Compensation in the Options menu disables Hardware Latency. Restored value, hidden-state updates and audible behavior on re-enabling are unknown.

Required quantitative audio/MIDI, gain, phase, metering, conversion and latency outcomes for External Audio Effect remain unknown. The documentary role descriptions and stored class presence provide no numerical oracle or internal mechanism.

Required boundary, automation, transport, persistence, undo, malformed, cancellation, disconnect, sample-rate failure, bypass, ownership, recovery and teardown outcomes for External Audio Effect remain unknown. Existing common-device, export and finite mix contracts do not establish these external-route interactions.

External Instrument sends MIDI and returns audio for external synthesizers or multitimbral plug-ins. For a physical destination, the upper MIDI To chooser selects the MIDI port and the lower chooser supplies MIDI channel numbers. No channel domain or wire encoding is specified here.

When another Set track contains a qualifying multitimbral plug-in, the upper MIDI To chooser can select that track and the lower chooser selects a specific MIDI channel in that plug-in. Arbitrary plug-in support is not established.

For a hardware synthesizer, Audio From selects interface inputs connected to the synthesizer outputs. Available choices depend on Audio Settings. This section does not independently establish a Configure… entry in this chooser.

For a qualifying multitimbral plug-in on another track, Audio From lists the plug-in auxiliary outputs. Its main outputs are heard on the track that contains the instrument. This does not specify channel matrices, gain or summing.
Gain adjusts the audio returning from the selected sound source. The section specifies no separate MIDI-send gain, amplitude law, legal range or clipping limiter.

For external hardware, Hardware Latency permits manual compensation of delay Live cannot automatically detect, using milliseconds or samples. Sample fine tuning and switching back to milliseconds before changing rate is guidance; no conversion or rounding is specified.
With a hardware route and Hardware Latency in samples, the specified sample count is retained when the sample rate changes. This does not establish physical alignment or event latency.
With a hardware route and Hardware Latency in milliseconds, the specified duration is retained when the sample rate changes. No sample conversion or numerical rounding law is established.

For internal routing, latency introduced by devices within Live is documented as automatically compensated, and External Instrument Hardware Latency is disabled. Its timing accuracy, limits and algorithm remain ungraded; this is not an internal mechanism requirement.

Unchecking Delay Compensation in Options disables Hardware Latency. The internal-route restriction also applies; neither statement promises a physical route is always editable under every other condition.

Required quantitative audio/MIDI, gain, phase, metering, conversion and latency outcomes for External Instrument remain unknown. The documentary role descriptions and stored class presence provide no numerical oracle or internal mechanism.

Required boundary, automation, transport, persistence, undo, malformed, cancellation, disconnect, sample-rate failure, bypass, ownership, recovery and teardown outcomes for External Instrument remain unknown. Existing common-device, export and finite mix contracts do not establish these external-route interactions.
